Ops AI by Chanl AI · Architecture and install guide

Ops AI architecture and installation guide

This guide is for the architects, DBAs, security reviewers and operators of a team that runs Ops AI on its own infrastructure. It says what each part does, how work moves through them, where data is kept and how it is kept apart, how the platform is secured, how to deploy and run it, and which parts are built today and which are still to come.

Each status in this guide is read from the code of the release it ships with. Built means it runs and is tested; Partial means some of it runs and the rest is named; Planned means designed and not yet in the code.

Runs on PostgreSQL 15 or newer Install with one script: git clone, then ./install.sh Docker Compose on Linux (x86-64 or ARM64), or Kubernetes Sign-in with OIDC, SAML or password SQL Server 2025 and Azure SQL: each service's stores tested on it; a full install not yet proven Team isolation inside the database: files and documents so far

1Overview

Routine work fills your team's day

An operations team spends its day on work that follows a pattern. A court notice arrives and someone opens a case, a complaint email needs triage, an account needs a hold, or a colleague asks what the procedure says. Software could do the reading and drafting. In a regulated business, though, software cannot change a customer's account unless a person decides, and every step has to leave a record that an auditor can read.

Why one-off automations fall short

Without a platform that carries those controls, each automation is a one-off script, or a pilot that your risk function has to review from scratch. Your team keeps retyping the same request across systems, and someone rebuilds the audit answer by hand each time it is asked for.

What Ops AI does

Ops AI is an operational AI platform that hands routine back-office work to software. Your team decides which changes to its other systems wait for a person, such as anything that moves money, and every step leaves a record. It runs on your own infrastructure, against a database your DBA controls and a model endpoint you choose. Nothing calls home.

In three parts

Agents

a configured model with instructions, tools, knowledge, skills and guardrails. It decides its own next step inside the limits it was given. People reach it through chat, other systems through the API.

Workflows

a versioned graph of typed steps that runs the same way every time and journals each step. It survives a crash without repeating a write, and waits days for a person at no cost.

Shared services and gateways

reviews and human tasks, cases, knowledge, files, documents, identity and audit, used by both. Every call to your systems leaves through the data gateway, every model call through the AI gateway.

The platform in one picture

Read it from the top: where work comes in, what runs it, and the one way out to your systems.

  • Where work comes from: People, mailboxes, other systems and AI assistants

    • A team mailbox: An outage report reaches a utility's service desk
    • Another system, over the API: A claims system opens a case
    • An AI assistant, over MCP: Every write it asks for waits for a person
  • Two ways to run work: An agent can be a workflow step, and a workflow can be an agent's tool

    • Workflows: Typed steps that run the same way every time, each one journaled
  • Shared services: Used by both, stored in your own database
    • Reviews, human tasks, cases
    • Knowledge, files, documents
    • Identity, teams, roles, audit
    • PostgreSQL: The database your DBA controls
  • Gateways, the only way out: Nothing reaches your systems or a model any other way

  • Your systems and your model

Principles behind the design

IdeaWhat it means for you
Agents and workflows are two ways of running workAn agent decides its own next step inside the limits it was given. A workflow runs fixed steps and survives a crash without repeating a write. Each works without the other, and they meet only through their public APIs: a workflow step can call an agent, and an agent can start a published workflow as a tool
A person approves the writes that matterA team chooses which writes wait for a person: every write, the writes of some apps, or one tool's. A write that waits needs an approval token bound to the exact input the reviewer saw; changing one character of the input after approval voids it
Two gateways are the only way outTool calls go through the data gateway, which checks the approval, the policy and an allow-list of hosts. Model calls go through the AI gateway, which checks the caller's key, budget and the data's sensitivity
Use cases are configurationA new process is workflows, document types, agents, tools and settings that a builder configures and publishes. No use case needs new code or a new screen. The court order notice used in this guide is one worked example among several
A team is the data boundaryAgents, workflows, knowledge and the work they produce belong to a team. Roles decide what a person may do inside the teams they belong to
Every change is versioned and reviewedAgents, workflows, skills, guardrails, task types and tool modules are published as immutable versions through a review by a second person. A running case keeps the version it started on

Words used in this guide

WordMeaning
TenantYour organisation's installation boundary. Every row of data carries its tenant
TeamA group of people that owns agents, workflows, knowledge and cases
AgentA configured model with instructions, tools, knowledge, skills and guardrails
WorkflowA versioned graph of typed steps: triggers, data steps, AI steps, human tasks, tool calls, cases
RunOne piece of work by an agent or a workflow, with a status, a budget and a journal
ThreadA conversation or a case's history; holds the saved state a run resumes from
Review, human taskA request for a person to decide something; the decision resumes the waiting run
CaseThe record of one piece of work for people: what it is about, what it waits on, what happened
ToolOne operation on one of your systems, such as "get account" or "place hold", with its access class (read or write) and approval policy
AliasA name such as default that points at a provider's model; changing the alias changes the model without changing an agent

What success looks like

A builder configures a new process by writing its agents and workflows and publishing them through a second person's review, and the team can start using them the same day. When the risk team asks about a change, the answer is already on the record: who approved it, which version ran and what it could reach.

2What runs

Ops AI ships as twelve long-running containers and one one-shot job: eight Python services built from one base image, the workflow worker (the agents image with another command), the web console, a policy engine (Open Policy Agent) and one entry point (Caddy). PostgreSQL is yours and runs outside them. Kubernetes runs the same images as the same workloads.

The containers

ContainerWhat it doesWhat it storesWhat it calls

consoleThe web console people useNothingThe APIs, from the browser through the proxy
platformSign-in and sessions, tenants, teams, members, roles, API keys, team policies, the audit log. The only issuer of sign-in tokensTenants, teams, users, members, roles, sessions, API keys, sign-in providers and domains, password hashes, audit entriesYour identity provider (OIDC or SAML); your mail server for invites and password resets

workerRuns workflow steps from the work queue, resumes runs after a decision, fires timers, reads team mailboxesSame database as agentsSame as agents
toolsThe data gateway: tool modules and their operations, connections, the approval check, the outbound allow-list, stored credentials, the call log, an MCP endpoint for AI assistantsTool modules and versions, connections and their tokens, credentials (encrypted), allow-list, call logYour systems (only hosts on the allow-list); opa; runner, for code tools; models, for the optional check before sending; platform, for team policies
runnerRuns a code tool's Python function in a WebAssembly sandbox with a memory cap, a time limit, no network, no files and no secrets. The function reaches other systems only by calling a tool back through toolsNothingtools, and only tools calls it

Every image runs as a non-root user (uid 10001). The Python images share one base layer of about 626 MB; the console image is about 440 MB.

Rules every service follows

RuleConsequence
A service reads only its own tablesEach service has its own database login and its own migration history. Data from another service comes through that service's API
Calls between services carry a signed service tokenEach service signs with its own key and is trusted only for the calls it is allowed to make. A service holds only the keys it uses
Every request is authenticatedEach service checks the caller's token against platform-service's published keys, so a request that skips the proxy is still refused
Every service refuses a schema behind itA service whose database has not been upgraded to its version stops at start and says which upgrade is missing
Settings come from the environment or a secrets fileAny setting may be a file under /run/secrets named after it. No image holds a secret

Not in the containers

ItemState
The databaseYours: PostgreSQL 15 or newer, or Azure Database for PostgreSQL 16 or newer. Azure SQL is in Azure SQL
A malware scannerThe files service has a hook a scanner calls back on, and a built-in test engine that recognises only the EICAR test file. A production scanner is yours to connect
The app that serves chat widgets on your other sitesPlanned as its own image. Widgets are configured and published in the console today
One process with no container runtimePlanned The services already run together in one process inside an all-in-one image, which the release package does not include

3How work flows

A reviewer will ask what the AI did

An agent that can change a customer's account is only useful if you can say exactly what it did, who approved it and what happens when something fails halfway. Most agent tools cannot answer that, so teams put a person in every step or hold the pilot back. This page follows three real flows from start to finish: a person chats with an agent that wants to change something, a workflow pauses for a person and resumes days later, and an email becomes cases that people decide. The release's automated use cases run each of these flows end to end.

Why the answers matter

Without this picture you cannot tell a reviewer where an approval is enforced, or what a crash does to a half-finished write. The answers are the same in all three flows. A write that needs approval waits for a token tied to its exact input. Every outside call goes through a gateway, and Ops AI saves a run's state after each step, so a crash or a restart loses nothing.

Run the flows yourself

To run the flows yourself, start at Build with Ops AI.

A chat turn with a tool approval

A member of the operations team asks the team's agent to place a hold on an account. Reading data needs no approval. Placing the hold changes data, and this team has set holds to wait for a reviewer, so the agent drafts the hold and a person approves it before anything reaches the core system.

  1. Person → Agent: Sends a message, signed in
  2. Agent → AI gateway: Model call on the agent's alias and key
  3. AI gateway → Agent: Asks for get_account, then place_hold
  4. Agent → Data gateway: get_account, a read
  5. Data gateway → Your core system: Calls an allow-listed host over HTTPS; the balance and holds come back and are logged
  6. Agent → Person: place_hold is a write, so the run pauses with its state saved and an approval card shows the exact input
    • The person sees the input that will be sent before approving it. Who may approve is the operation's policy: the number of approvers, the team they belong to, whether a fresh sign-in is needed, and whether the person who asked may decide.
  7. Person → Agent: Approves, with a fresh sign-in if asked; the token is bound to the input's hash, the tool and the step
  8. Agent → Data gateway: place_hold with the token; the policy engine checks it is signed, for the same input, not expired and has enough approvers
  9. Data gateway → Your core system: Sends the call with the stored credential; the hold is placed
  10. Data gateway → Agent: The result, recorded once by its key
  11. Agent → AI gateway: Model call with the result
  12. Agent → Person: The answer, streamed
StepWhat protects it
The messageThe person's sign-in token names the tenant and team; nothing in the message can change them
The model callThe AI gateway checks the agent's key, its budget and the data's sensitivity before it calls your model endpoint
The pauseThe approval waits in the conversation with its state saved; closing the browser loses nothing
The writeThe data gateway refuses a call whose input differs from what was approved by a single character, a token past its 15 minutes, or a token from a run that another process has since taken over
A repeatA retried call with the same idempotency key returns the first result and writes nothing

A workflow run with a human task

A workflow starts from an API call, an email or an event from another service. The worker runs its steps in order and saves each one. When a step needs a person, the run pauses and holds on to no worker. When the person decides, the run goes back on the queue.

SituationWhat happens
A worker dies mid-stepIts lease expires after 15 seconds. Another worker takes the run, raises the lease generation, and continues from the last saved step. A write the first worker already made is found by its key and not made again; anything the first worker sends afterwards is refused as stale
The task's deadline passesThe task shows as overdue, or, when the step says so, the run leaves on its timeout path, for example to escalate. A timeout never approves anything
A step fails three timesThe run fails with the error on its record, and its case shows the failure to people
The workflow is republished mid-runThe run keeps the version it started on; new runs take the new version

Email to case: a court order notice

This is one worked example. A team connects its mailbox and publishes three workflows through review. From then on, every notice that a court or tax authority emails to the bank, ordering it to hold or pay a customer's funds, is read, checked, turned into cases and answered. None of this is code written for court orders, because the document type, the workflows, the tools and the task types are all configuration.

ConfigurationWhat it holds
The mailboxProvider, folder, the credential's name in the credential store, and the address replies come from
A document type, "court order notice"The fields to read, their checks, the score floor, and the examples corrections have taught it
Three workflowsMailed documents (one run per message), Mailed document (one per attachment), Court order case (one per debtor)
ToolsSearch customers, list accounts, place hold, add a note, send a reply: operations on your systems with their approval policies
Task typesCheck the read, hold or flag, send the acknowledgement: what the person sees and the actions they can take

Other worked examples in the release use the same parts: complaint email triage, a hold requested through the API, and a customer summary built from the core system and an agent.

What success looks like

You can point at any run and say which version ran, what each step received and returned, who approved the write and what they saw when they did. A crash, a retry or a week-long wait changes none of that.

4Build with Ops AI

This guide starts with a single chat message and ends with an agent and a workflow that call each other, in seven steps you can run yourself.

Where to begin when you are new to Ops AI

If you are new to Ops AI, you may already have an agent or a workflow in mind without knowing where to begin. Each of the pieces you will use (chat, knowledge, tools, agents and workflows) has its own page, and each of those pages assumes you have read the one before it.

This guide takes you through the pieces in order, in seven short steps. You run each step from the Ops AI command line, and the same calls are available in the Python and TypeScript SDKs. Every step links to a runnable example folder in the repository that you can copy, and those examples are tested on every change.

The plan

  1. Talk to it. Send one chat message, then add a knowledge page.
  2. Give it a tool. Run one read operation, first in Mock and then for real.
  3. Make an agent and a workflow. You apply each one from a file.
  4. Make them call each other. A workflow step asks an agent a question, and an agent starts a workflow.

Before you start

You needHow
An install you can sign in toYour company's Ops AI, or one on your machine from the Quickstart
The command lineInstall the CLI, then opsai login
The Builder role in a teamBuilders create agents, workflows and knowledge bases

Try it

Run the steps in order. Before each one, open its example folder and copy the files and ids that its command names, such as agent.yaml, workflow.yaml and request.json.

  1. Chat. Send one message and read the reply. opsai chat say -m "What can you help me with?" (example)
  2. Knowledge. Add one page to a knowledge base and search it. opsai kb add-text kb_... --title "ATM limits" --text "The daily limit is 500 dollars.", then opsai kb search kb_... "What is the daily limit?" (example)
  3. Tool. Run one read operation in Mock, then for real. opsai tools run <app> <tool> --input id=42, then the same with --real (example)
  4. Agent. Apply an agent from a file, publish it, and ask it one question. opsai agents apply agent.yaml, opsai agents publish <id>, opsai agents chat <id> --message "..." (example)
  5. Workflow. Validate, apply and test-run a three-step workflow. opsai workflows validate workflow.yaml, opsai workflows apply workflow.yaml, opsai workflows run <id> --input request.json (example)
  6. A workflow asks an agent. An Agent step calls a published agent and keeps the answer it gives, along with its citations (example).
  7. An agent starts a workflow. A chat calls a published workflow as one of its tools (example).

What success looks like

At each step, the command prints the record it created or the answer it received. When a step is refused, the command tells you why. For example, if a workflow input is missing a required field, the message names that field. Once you have finished step 7, you have a chat that starts a published workflow and a workflow step that asks a published agent.

Why the order matters

If you skip ahead, you may build your first agent before you have run your first tool. A failure in one piece then looks like a failure in all of them. Because each step is small, a failure that happens along the way points you to the piece that caused it.

The workflows and agents pages list every further example, including approvals, checklists, delegation and evaluations.

How agents and workflows meet

Agents and workflows call each other only through their public APIs. That means you can use either one on its own, without the other.

  • A workflow asks an agent: Step 6 above
    • How: An Agent step names a published agent and maps the prompt from the run's data
    • What runs: The agent's published version
    • What comes back: The agent's final answer, as the step's output
  • An agent starts a workflow: Step 7 above
    • How: The workflow is on the agent's published tool list
    • What runs: The workflow's live version, for the signed-in person
    • What comes back: The run's result, or a handle when the run waits for a person

5Workflows

A process that depends on who is at the desk

Suppose you must open a case for each court order, place a hold only after a person approves it, and reply on the channel the request arrived on. If people do these steps by hand, each step varies with who does it, and the record ends up in an email thread. If a script does them, a crash halfway can repeat a change to a customer's account.

What it costs to leave it manual

Without a workflow, every request is retyped across systems, approvals get lost between inboxes, and someone rebuilds the audit answer by hand. A workflow is a versioned graph of typed steps that removes that work. Each step's input and output is saved as it runs, so a crash or a restart loses nothing and a write is never made twice. Some steps run an AI task, such as an agent, a classification or an extraction. The other steps apply rules, call tools or wait for a person to decide. Rows marked planned on this page are designed and not yet built.

Route a support message with an AI step

The Quickstart writes a three-step workflow and runs it. This one adds an AI step. It sorts a support message into billing or technical, and sends it out by otherwise when its confidence is below 0.6. Save it as route.yaml:

schemaVersion: 2
id: route_support_message
name: Route an inbound support message
nodes:
- {id: start, type: ops.trigger.request, typeVersion: 1, name: Message,
   parameters: {inputSchema: {type: object, required: [text], properties: {text: {type: string}}}}}
- id: sort
  type: ops.ai.classify
  typeVersion: 1
  name: Classify
  parameters:
    text: $.input.text
    categories:
    - {name: billing, description: "invoices, charges, refunds"}
    - {name: technical, description: "login, outage, app"}
    minConfidence: 0.6
- {id: billing, type: ops.flow.end, typeVersion: 1, name: Billing, parameters: {outcome: billing}}
- {id: technical, type: ops.flow.end, typeVersion: 1, name: Technical, parameters: {outcome: technical}}
- {id: other, type: ops.flow.end, typeVersion: 1, name: Other, parameters: {outcome: other}}
- {id: failed, type: ops.flow.end, typeVersion: 1, name: Failed, parameters: {outcome: classify_failed, result: failed}}
connections:
- {from: {node: start, port: payload}, to: {node: sort, port: in}}
- {from: {node: sort, port: billing}, to: {node: billing, port: in}}
- {from: {node: sort, port: technical}, to: {node: technical, port: in}}
- {from: {node: sort, port: otherwise}, to: {node: other, port: in}}
- {from: {node: sort, port: error}, to: {node: failed, port: in}}
opsai workflows validate route.yaml
opsai workflows apply route.yaml
opsai workflows run route_support_message --wait --input '{"text": "I was charged twice this month."}'
flowchart TD
  A[Message arrives] --> B[Classify]
  B -->|Billing| C[billing]
  B -->|Technical| D[technical]
  B -->|Below 0.6| E[other]

The sample message ends with the outcome billing. A model answer outside the categories leaves by error and ends as classify_failed. opsai workflows types lists every step type with its ports and settings.

You do not need the console to build a workflow, but it shows and edits the same graph under Build › Workflows. Open a workflow step and pick a field shows how to read and fill one step there.

From draft to live run

Every command reads its address and sign-in from your profile (Install the command line).

StepCommandWhat it does
Checkopsai workflows validate workflow.yamlLists every problem, each with its path, code, message and a suggestion
Save a draftopsai workflows apply workflow.yamlCreates or updates the draft
Save a working copyopsai workflows save-copy <id> workflow.yamlSaves it as the workflow's working copy, problems and all, and makes no version; refused with stale_base when someone saved since you read it
See what changedopsai workflows diff <id> --from live --to working-copyEach step added, removed, changed (with its settings) or moved
Publishopsai workflows publish <id> --note "Ready"Requests the publish of the newest draft; a second person reviews it unless the team's publish policy says otherwise. With --working-copy it makes the next version from the working copy and requests its publish in one call, refused before any version is made while publish-preview lists a blocker
Runopsai workflows run <id> --input input.json --waitStarts a test run and waits for it to end; --live makes a live run
Test from fixturesopsai workflows test <folder>Runs every fixture case in a folder
Look at a runopsai workflows inspect <run-id>, opsai workflows trace <run-id>The run, and its timeline step by step
Decide a taskopsai workflows decide <task-id> approveAnswers the human task a run waits on
Retryopsai workflows retry <run-id>Retries a stuck run from its last recorded step
Redriveopsai runs redrive <run-id>, opsai runs bulk redrive --code tool_failedRuns a Failed or Stuck run again from the step that failed, on the version it started on, once you have fixed the cause. Steps that finished return what they recorded and run nothing. A failed write is sent again, on its earlier approval, only when its answer proves it did nothing; any other is settled by the gateway's record first (recovery and redrive). bulk redrives or cancels every run of your team that a filter matches (workflow, kind, code, time)
Replay, fork, evaluateopsai workflows replay, fork, evalPlanned

From Python, it looks like this. TypeScript has the same method names on ops.workflows, and they take a parsed object or JSON:

from ops_ai import OpsAI

ops = OpsAI()
check = ops.workflows.validate("workflow.yaml")
check.raise_for_errors()
draft = ops.workflows.apply("workflow.yaml")
ops.workflows.publish(draft["workflowId"], note="Ready")
run = ops.workflows.run(draft["workflowId"], input={"customerEmail": "ada@example.test"}, wait=True)

A new run is a test run unless you ask for a live one (mode="live", or --live). A test run signs in with the app's sandbox account when it has one, and with its live account otherwise (Tools and apps).

A run keeps the version it started on. Publishing a new version changes only the runs that start after it.

What a definition holds

A definition has an id, a name, a list of nodes and a list of connections. Each node has a type, a typeVersion, its parameters and a stable id; each connection joins one node's output port to another's input. opsai workflows types prints every step type with its ports and parameter schema.

When something goes wrong

What you seeWhereWhat to do
The graph is invalidvalidate lists each problem with path, code, message and suggestionFix the node or field it names
409 not_liveA live run of a workflow with no published versionPublish first
422 on startThe input does not match the request trigger's schemaSend the trigger's required fields
A step was refusedrun.error, and run.failure.nodeId names the stepFix the tool, the mapping or the input
status=waiting with a taskIdThe run waits for a personDecide it in Human Tasks, or opsai workflows decide <task-id> approve

Run a workflow on a schedule

In the console, see Schedule a workflow or an agent. From a terminal or a script:

A workflow that starts with the Schedule trigger can run by itself: every 15 minutes, every day at 07:30, or weekdays between 07:00 and 18:00 in a time zone. The schedule is saved on the trigger step, outside the workflow's versions, so it applies to the live version at once with no publish. A tick whose last scheduled run is still going is skipped and shown in the trigger's log with the reason. Pause stops the ticks; Resume waits for the next slot. A scheduled run sends only dueAt, so the trigger's input schema may require nothing else (a save naming another field is refused with 422), and the workflow needs a team. The shortest interval is the install's schedule_floor_minutes, 5 by default, and a rule under it is refused with "At least 5 minutes on this install."; raising it leaves saved schedules running, and each is refused at its next save. After the clock was down, the latest slot runs once, marked late, if it is within half the smaller gap to the slot before or after it (and at least 90 seconds); an older one is shown as missed. A rule saved just before its slot runs that slot. Reading a schedule needs the right to view the team's workflows; clearing one works even when a newer version dropped the step, and the workflow's view says when a schedule is idle and why.

From a script or a terminal (step is the trigger step's id):

opsai workflows schedule kinds                                  # the rule kinds and their labels
opsai workflows schedule preview --kind every --set every=15 --set unit=minutes --set tz=Europe/London
opsai workflows schedule save held_wires --step start --kind every \
  --set every=15 --set unit=minutes --set start=07:00 --set tz=Europe/London \
  --set 'days=["mon","tue","wed","thu","fri"]'
opsai workflows schedule show held_wires --step start           # the rule in words, the next runs, the last outcome
opsai workflows schedule clear held_wires --step start

--rule '{"kind": "every", ...}' (or @file.json) passes the whole rule instead of --kind and --set. Each --set value is read as JSON when it parses, otherwise as text. The words and next runs come from the server, so the console and the command line say the same thing.

What success looks like

A run ends with an outcome you named, and its timeline shows every step with its input and output. A step that needs a person pauses the run at no cost until they decide. A new version changes only the runs that start after it.

Agents

6Agents

Some work never follows the same steps twice

A staff member asks a question, or a request needs a few lookups before anyone knows what to do. A fixed script cannot cover that, and a loose chatbot with no limits cannot be trusted near a customer's account. Without something in between, the team keeps answering the same questions by hand.

An agent is a model with instructions, tools, knowledge, skills, guardrails and a budget, and inside those limits it chooses its own next step. You can reach it through chat or the API, and a workflow can call it with an agent step. If you give an agent no budget, no approval on its writes and no access to your documents, it has to guess. A risk review will stop a guess that changes a customer's account.

Write and test your first agent

Save this as agent.yaml:

name: Account opening helper
role: answer
instructions: Answer from these instructions only. Business accounts need two identity documents.
memory:
  enabled: false

Then save it as a draft and test it before anyone publishes it:

opsai agents validate agent.yaml
opsai agents apply agent.yaml                 # prints the agent's id
opsai agents test <agent-id> --message "What documents open a business account?"

The same agent opens under Build › Agents in the console, where its Test panel runs the same turn.

What an agent is made of

Rows marked planned are designed and not yet built.

PartWhat it doesStatus
InstructionsWhat the agent is for and how it answersBuilt
ModelThe model alias it runs on. Changing what an alias points at changes the model without changing the agentBuilt
ToolsOperations on your systems it may call. Each keeps its own approval setting, so a write can wait for a person (Tools and apps)Built
KnowledgeKnowledge bases it may search; answers cite page and section (Knowledge)Built
SkillsReusable instructions it loads when a request matches; always-on skills are in every turnBuilt Skill tests, generation and import planned
GuardrailsTopics it must refuse, checked on the question and on the answer; the reply names the guardrailBuilt for blocked topics. Other kinds planned
BudgetThe most model calls and tool calls in one turn; the reply says when it stoppedBuilt

Write the instructions as a brief

The agent page writes the prompt from headings, so each kind of instruction has one place. Job, How to answer, Hand off when, Examples and Never are always there. How to answer holds what an answer includes and how it is formatted; tone goes in its own section.

Add section opens a searchable list. Sections sit in groups (Voice and style, Context, Behaviour), each with an example line, and one already added is greyed out and checked. The workspace decides what the list holds: Personality, Tone, Environment, Context, Tool use, Error handling and Escalation wording to start, and a section you do not fill in is left out of the prompt. Tone and Personality offer preset chips (Warm, Neutral, Formal, Concise, Plain-spoken): pressing one writes its sentence into the section as ordinary text you can edit. Add custom section asks for a name first and adds a heading of your own, up to five. A custom name cannot repeat a heading the brief already has or another custom name, and it is marked prompt text only: nothing else reads it. People who can only view an agent see the sections and no Add section or Remove controls.

An admin changes the list under Settings, Agent instructions: rename a section, move it up or down, hide it from Add section, add one, and edit its hint, example line, menu group and presets, then Save. Reset to default puts the first list back. Changing the list never rewrites an agent already saved; the new labels and order apply the next time that agent's brief is saved. People without the settings manage right read the list and have no controls.

View prompt shows what the model receives, in this order: Who you are, Goal, Personality, Tone, Environment, Context, How to answer, Tool use, Error handling, your own sections in the order you keep them, Hand off when, Escalation wording, Examples, and Never last, when the list is the default; an admin's order replaces it. Escalation wording sits straight after Hand off when so the moment and the words stay together, and Context sits straight after Environment. An agent saved before sections reads and runs exactly as it did.

Sources for the headings (what each gave us):

  • ElevenLabs, https://elevenlabs.io/docs/agents-platform/best-practices/prompting-guide: separate Personality, Environment, Tone, Goal, Tools, Error handling and Escalation sections; tone kept in one place.
  • Vapi, https://docs.vapi.ai/prompting-guide: identity, response guidelines, context and examples that include an error case.
  • OpenAI, https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering: identity, instructions, examples and context under markdown headers.

From draft to published agent

StepCommandWhat it does
Checkopsai agents validate agent.yamlChecks the file and lists every problem
Save a draftopsai agents apply agent.yamlCreates or updates the draft
Try the draftopsai agents test <id> --message "..."One test turn, as the Test panel runs it
Publishopsai agents publish <id> --note "Ready"Requests the publish. A second person reviews it unless the team's publish policy says otherwise
Chatopsai agents chat <id> --message "..."One message to the published agent
Runopsai agents run <id> --message "..." --mode waitStarts the published agent and waits; --mode stream streams the answer, --mode background returns at once
Look backopsai agents trace <id>The agent's recent runs

A published version does not change. Editing makes a new draft, and a conversation already under way keeps the version it started on.

From Python:

from ops_ai import OpsAI

ops = OpsAI()
draft = ops.agents.apply("agent.yaml")
ops.agents.chat(draft["id"], "What documents open a business account?")

ops.agents.eval(id, cases) scores a set of cases against a published agent from Python. An opsai agents eval command, and the run and eval methods in the TypeScript SDK, are planned.

A background run lives in the program that started it and is lost if that program exits before the reply is on the thread. opsai agents run --mode background exits as soon as it prints the ids, so its run is lost. Use background mode from a program that keeps running. Runs that carry on without the caller are planned.

ops.agents.schedule(id, message, due_at=...) arms one run for a due time, and the same key runs only once. Repeating schedules are planned.

Agent examples shows each of these in Python, TypeScript and the command line.

Choosing between an agent and a workflow

  • Are the steps the same every time?
    • No, a person asks and the steps vary: An agent in chat.
      • Should it be able to start a governed process?
        • Yes: Publish the workflow and give it to the agent as a tool.
        • No: The agent in chat is enough.
    • Yes, with a record and a person deciding: A workflow.
    • Mostly, with one judgement in the middle: A workflow with an Agent step; the step returns what the agent's output schema says.

When an agent drafts a write that needs approval, the chat shows Approve and Reject, and approving may ask for your password again (Human tasks and approvals).

What success looks like

Your agent answers from its instructions and cites the page and section of your documents. A change that needs approval waits for a person before it reaches your system. Your published version stays as it was while you edit the next one.

Run an agent on a schedule

An agent runs on a schedule through a workflow with the agent as its step: from the agent's Channels tab, Schedule (Run on a schedule) makes that workflow and saves its schedule, and publishing it starts the runs. There is no separate schedule route for an agent, so a script makes the same workflow. The steps are in Schedule a workflow or an agent.

Chat and channels

7The Ops Assistant

This page shows how your staff can ask for work in plain words in a chat, and how other systems can reach the same agents without a person passing the request along.

Why teams ask in chat, and why systems need a way in too

An operations team fields the same questions all day: which customers have a dispute open, what the branch cash limit is, who owns a case. A claims handler asks which policy applies, and a lender's analyst asks where a loan stands. Answering each one by hand means opening three systems and copying the result across. Another system that needs the same answer has no way in unless a person relays it.

A chat is a conversation with one of your team's agents or with the team's Ops Assistant. The assistant looks things up in your team's apps and replies with what it read. A channel is the route by which that conversation, or a workflow run, arrives. Without channels, each new way of asking, from a mailbox to an API call, would need its own copy of the agent and its own set of rules.

From question to action

  1. Ask. Open Chat and type your question the way you would say it out loud.
  2. Check the answer and its sources. The reply streams in, along with the passages and tool results it drew on.
  3. Approve any change. When the answer needs a change in an app, the assistant reads the change back to you and makes it only after you choose Save.
  4. Connect other channels. Point a mailbox, the HTTP API or a due date at the same agent, so work can start without anyone typing.

Ask your first question

Open Chat in the console and ask a question. You can also ask from the command line:

opsai chat say -m "Which customers have a card dispute open?"
opsai chat say --agent "Branch policy" --test -m "What is the daily cash limit at a branch?"
opsai chat say --thread <thread-id> -m "And who owns the first one?"

The reply streams in with its sources, and the command prints a link to the same conversation in the console. Because the assistant acts as you, it can reach only what your own sign-in allows.

Where requests can come from

ChannelWhat comes inStatus
The console's chatPeople chatting with the team's agents and the Ops AssistantBuilt
A chat on your own pagesThe same chat in an iframe on an intranet page (Chat on your own pages)Built the installer does not run it yet
A team mailboxEmails that start a workflow, read once each, over IMAP, Gmail or Microsoft 365; replies go from the mailbox's addressBuilt
The HTTP APIOther systems starting a run or an agent with a team API keyBuilt
MCPAI assistants calling the team's toolsPartial read tools, as test runs
A due timeA run that starts when a date passesBuilt A recurring schedule is planned
A webhook from another systemA signed incoming request that starts a runPlanned

What you can do in a chat

A checklist for longer requests

When a request needs several lookups, more than one app, or a change, the assistant shows a short checklist above the answer. It ticks off each step as it finishes it.

When you need to sign in to an app

If a step needs an app you have not connected yet, the assistant pauses at that step and shows a Connect card. Press it and sign in, and the chat picks up again at the same step, so you do not need to retype anything.

Think harder

When a reply needed a plan or several lookups, it offers Think harder. Pressing it answers the same question again using the deeper model. You get the same result by writing "think harder" in a message, either on its own or alongside your question.

Approving a change to an app

Before the assistant changes anything in an app, it reads the change back to you, and it makes the change only after you choose Save. Until you do, nothing in the app has changed.

Follow-up questions

  • For 5 minutes, a chat reuses what it has already read from an app with your own sign-in, so follow-up questions are answered faster. It does not reuse a read made on the team's account, because the team's account may see different records from the ones you can see. The reply tells you when it used an earlier read. Saving a change to that app clears the reused reads, so the next lookup reads the app afresh.
  • Under a reply, short suggestion chips offer likely next questions. Press one to ask it.
  • The assistant may suggest things to remember, but it asks you first. It does not store a memory without asking.

Files you attach

When you attach a file in a chat, it is read once and the assistant receives its full text, up to about 24,000 characters for that turn. This works for scanned pages, partly scanned pages, images of text and filled-in forms, including the typed values in a form's fields. Scans are read by OCR, so a long scan can take a moment before the assistant answers. If a file is longer than the limit, or could not be read, the reply tells you so in plain words.

When no source matches your question

If no knowledge passage matched your question, the reply still keeps its lists and paragraphs, and a note appears under it: "No knowledge passage matched this question." The reply is often a complete answer anyway, such as a question back to you or a plan.

The assistant states facts about your organisation (policies, processes, timelines, fees, products, teams, customers) only when your knowledge or a tool result in the chat supports them. When neither does, it tells you it does not have that information and suggests what it can do instead. If a reply that draws on knowledge is missing its source numbers, a check adds them. That check does not replace a correct answer with "nothing found".

Choosing apps and accounts

  • A chat uses the apps your team has turned on. You can use the Connectors button in the chat box to leave an app out of a chat, either before you start or partway through.
  • The button shows the icons of the apps in use, up to four and then a count. The list stays open while you tick and untick apps, and each row shows the app's icon. If an app needs your sign-in, its row has a Connect button.
  • If you have two accounts for the same app connected and neither is the default, the assistant asks which one to use. The one you pick becomes the default for any call that does not name an account.
  • If your team has turned an app off, you see a card with Ask an admin.

You manage your sign-ins on Apps › Mine (Apps).

When this is working

A member of staff asks a question in the console, and the reply streams in with its sources, drawing only on what that person's own sign-in allows. Any change to an app waits until they choose Save. Meanwhile a mailbox, the HTTP API or a due date can start the same agent without anyone typing.

Without chat and channels

Without a chat, each question becomes a ticket for a person who then opens the same three systems. Without channels, every system that needs an answer ends up with its own copy of the agent, and over time those copies drift apart.

8Apps

This page shows how your agents can look up a customer in the systems you already use and, once a person approves, change a record there.

Why agents need to reach your systems

Most of the work in an operations queue depends on data that lives in other systems. An operations team needs its agent to look up the customer, read the account and, once someone approves, place the hold. A claims team needs the policy and the open claim, and a lending team needs the loan balance before it can quote a payoff. If the agent can only hold a conversation, the person still does every one of those steps by hand, and the queue stays as long as it was.

Connecting agents to your systems without any checks creates a different problem. Each agent would carry its own keys and follow its own rules, nobody could say which account it signed in as, and a risk review would have no single place to read what it changed.

Ops AI solves this with apps and tools. An app is a system outside Ops AI that your agents and workflows work with, such as Salesforce, a core banking API or a mailbox. Each app brings a set of tools, and each tool is a single operation that an agent or a workflow step can carry out in that app, such as "get account" or "place hold". Every tool call leaves through one gateway, which checks who is calling, whether a person has approved the call, and which hosts it may reach.

How it works

  1. Turn an app on. A team admin picks the app and chooses who signs in to it.
  2. Check what its tools do. Each tool is marked read or write. You can run a tool against mock answers before it touches anything real.
  3. Decide which writes wait. Tools that only read run straight away. A team admin can make tools that write wait for a person, either for the whole team, for chosen apps or for one tool.
  4. Give the tools to an agent. The agent calls them in a chat or a workflow, and every call is recorded in the log.

Try it

From the command line you can see which apps your team has turned on, what one of them can do, and call one of its tools.

opsai apps list
opsai apps show <app-id>
opsai tools list --app <app-id>
opsai tools run <app-id> <tool> --input '{"accountId": "ACC-1001"}'
opsai tools run <app-id> <tool> --input '{"accountId": "ACC-1001"}' --real

By default, tools run replies from the tool's mock answers and sends nothing to the app. Adding --real sends the call as a test run, and it passes through every check the gateway applies.

The console has the same views under Data › Apps, which lists the team's apps, and Data › Tools. On a tool's page, Run offers two choices. Mock replies from the saved mock answers and sends nothing, while Real sends the request and shows you exactly what was sent, with every key hidden.

Turn an app on

  1. A team admin opens Data › Apps, view Team setup, and presses Turn on on the app's card.
  2. They choose who signs in, either Everyone uses the team's login or Each person signs in. Saving this choice does not sign anyone in yet.
  3. Pressing Sign in with my login or Sign in the team login opens the app's own sign-in page. Once a login has signed in, the app shows Connected.

Set up an app covers the full steps, the states an app can be in, how to bring your own OAuth app and how to turn an app off.

Who signs in: the team's login or each person's

For each app, a team admin decides whose login the tools use. The choice sits on the app's Settings tab under Who signs in, and the agent's Tools list shows the same answer beside each tool's app.

  • Everyone uses the team's login: Suits a shared mailbox.
    • Chat user sees: No sign-in and no question. Under the reply: "Runs in <app> as <login> (team login). You are recorded as the person who asked."
    • Audit keeps: The team login and the person who asked
  • Each person signs in: Suits a system that records who did what, such as a core banking API.
    • Chat user sees: The first time, one card: Sign in to <app> to continue. After signing in the chat carries on, and later actions in that app ask nothing
    • Audit keeps: The person's own login

Because the team admin makes this choice, nobody is asked in a chat or a Human Task to pick between their own login and the team's. Each person manages their own sign-ins in My apps.

When an app is set so that each person signs in, a run that nobody started, such as a schedule, cannot call it. There is no person for the run to act as, and the team's login is not used as a backup. Instead, the run is refused with a message that names the app and the two ways forward: set the app to Everyone uses the team's login, or have a person start the run. So that this does not surprise you later, saving a workflow that a schedule or an event starts warns you about each such step before its first run. Changing the answer needs the connections.manage permission, which team admins have by default.

LoginUsed byHow to add it
Team loginAnyone in the team. The Default account answers every live call that names no otherSign in the team login, by a team admin
Your loginTools you run, and agents acting for youSign in to in a chat, or My apps
Sandbox accountTest runs onlyAdd a sandbox account on the app's page

Your own sign-ins

You manage your own sign-ins on Apps › Mine, which you can also reach as My apps in the user menu. It shows one card for each app the team has turned on, with Connect, Reconnect or Add another account. If you have two accounts in one app and neither is set as the default, the assistant asks you which one to use.

What the gateway checks on every call

  • Accounts. When an agent acts for a person, it uses that person's own account, so it can reach only what that person is allowed to reach.
  • Sandbox and live. Test runs use an account marked Sandbox. Test runs include an agent's Test panel, a draft, and Real on a tool's page. Live runs never use a sandbox account. If an app has no sandbox account, a test run that writes asks the person before it goes ahead.
  • Reads and writes. Every tool is marked read or write. Writes run straight away until a team turns approvals on. After that, each write waits as a Human Task (Human tasks and approvals).
  • Secrets. Keys and passwords that a tool sends are stored encrypted and never shown again, and they are removed from whatever an app sends back. If you type a key into a tool's own header, saving the tool refuses it, because the app's account signs every call.
  • Allowed hosts. A tool can call only the hosts that a Security admin has allowed.
  • Call log. Every call is logged together with the account it ran as. An app's Logs tab shows its calls to the people who are allowed to read the log.

Where tools come from

SourceWhat you getStatus
A built-in or installed appThe app's tools, and sometimes resources: agents, skills, workflows and document types your team can copyBuilt
An OpenAPI 3.0 or 3.1 documentOne tool per operation, reviewed before useBuilt
An MCP serverIts tools, through the same gatewayBuilt
A tool written in the consoleA request on an app's address, with mock answers for tests (Build your first tool)Built
A Python function in a sandbox with no network, files or secretsA code toolPartial runs, writing one in the console is planned

Approvals

By default, a tool that writes runs straight away. A team admin can make writes wait for a person at three levels:

  • the whole team
  • the apps they pick
  • one tool, on the tool's page under Access and approval

When more than one level is set, the most specific one applies. Each level has three settings: don't ask, ask the person in the chat, or ask a reviewer. A write that waits becomes a Human Task (Human tasks and approvals).

Assistants over MCP

An AI assistant such as Claude or Cursor can call your team's tools over MCP. These calls pass through the same gateway as an agent's calls and count as test runs, so they use an app's sandbox account when the team has one.

What the assistant reachesWrites
The team's address lists the team's read tools onlyNone are listed
A link a builder made on Channels › MCP lists the tools and workflows picked for it, writes includedA write always waits for a person, whatever the team's approval settings say

There is one exception. An operation that only creates a draft, such as installing a template or starting a workflow, does not wait, because the draft still goes through its own review before it is published. Setup steps are on MCP.

Who may do what

ActionWho
Turn an app on or off, sign in its team login, set who signs in, add a custom appA team admin
Connect, set as default or disconnect your own accountAnyone in the team
Add or edit an auth config (the OAuth app an app signs in with)A team admin
Add, rotate or delete a secretA Security admin
Change approval settingsPeople who manage the team's reviews

Limits

  • Triggers that an app starts on a schedule or by polling, and signed incoming webhooks, are planned.
  • The team's MCP address lists read tools only. To write over MCP, an assistant needs a link, and every write waits for a person.

When your apps are set up well

Your team admin has turned on the apps the team uses, and each tool is marked read or write. An agent can read an account without asking anyone, and a write waits for a person once the team has turned approvals on. Because the app's Logs tab shows every call and the account it ran as, your risk review has one log to read.

The risk of going without the gateway

Without the gateway, each agent would hold its own keys. A single leaked key would expose every agent. A write could reach a customer's account with no person named against it, and finding out what an agent changed would mean searching through each agent's logs one by one.

9Data and database

Ops AI keeps everything in one PostgreSQL database. Each of the seven services that keep data owns its own tables, applies its own migration history and connects with its own login, which can read and write rows in that service's tables and nothing else. File bytes live outside the database, on a volume or in object storage.

Every table that holds customer data carries a tenant_id, and the team-owned ones a team_id. Each service also keeps one version table that records which of its migrations the database holds.

Tenants and teams

A tenant is your installation's organisation; a team is the data boundary inside it. Roles decide what a person may do inside a team; they never open another team's data.

BoundaryHow it is enforcedStatus
Tenant, from the sign-in tokenThe tenant always comes from the verified token or API key, never from a request body, header or parameter. A record of another tenant answers 404Built
Tenant, in the database, for agents and platformForced row-level security on 33 agents tables (including saved run state) and 18 platform tables: a row is visible only when its tenant_id equals the tenant the transaction set, and a transaction that set none sees nothing. The policies apply to the tables' owner tooBuilt
Tenant, in the database, for tools, models, kb, files and documentsEvery store query filters by tenant in the service's code. In tools-service, a connection's saved sign-ins (tokens and keys, sign-ins in progress, environment settings, connect links) are also held to their tenant and team by database policies, run as ops_tools_tenant; policies for the other tools tables and for models are still to comePartial
Background loopsThe agents service's lease sweeper, timer poller and thread inbox loops claim work before they know its tenant through one system role that may read across tenants; each then does the work under the row's own tenant. No request ever runs as that roleBuilt
Team, in the servicesEvery read of a team-owned table goes through one team filter in the store layer, so a person sees only the teams they belong to; another team's record answers 404Built
Team, in the databaseA database-level team policy beneath the store filter. 10Security and governance

When your risk review looks at an agent, it will want to know who signed in, what they were allowed to do, what an action that changes data needed before it ran, where a call was allowed to go and what was kept as evidence. This page shows you where each of those answers lives in Ops AI.

The pilot works, then the risk review asks

Picture a card team whose agent drafts dispute credits well. Then the reviewer asks who approved the credit, what the agent could reach, which hosts it called and where the record is kept. A claims team and a lender will be asked the same questions. If the answers live in each agent's code, every new use case has to wait for its own review. Worse, a single unreviewed change to a customer's account can be enough to end the programme.

Ops AI is designed so that software can draft any change, but only a person can let it through. The controls build on one another:

  • Sign-in establishes who you are.
  • Roles set what you may do in a team.
  • Approvals decide what a single action that changes data needs before it runs.
  • The gateways and the allow-list control where a call may go.
  • The audit records keep the evidence.

Setting up the controls

  1. Sign people in with your identity provider, or with a password if you have no provider.
  2. Give each person a role in each team. The role's grid says what that person may do.
  3. Choose which actions wait for a person, and how many approvers each one needs.
  4. Allow only the hosts your agents need. The outbound list starts empty, so nothing is reachable until you add a host.
  5. Hand the reviewer the evidence. Together, the audit log, the tool call log and the run journal show who did what, and when.

Check your own access

Start by seeing who you are signed in as and what your role allows, then look at which open tasks are waiting for a decision.

opsai people me
opsai people roles
opsai tasks list --view open

In the console you will find the same views in three places. Govern › Access shows roles and tool access, Govern › Policies holds approvals and the allow-list, and Settings › Approvals holds the approval settings.

Sign-in and SSO

MethodHow it worksStatus
OIDC single sign-onAuthorization code flow with PKCE (S256); asymmetric signing algorithms only; the issuer is pinned. Works with any OIDC provider, such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta, configured as a generic OIDC providerBuilt
SAML 2.0 single sign-onService-provider-initiated; signed responses required, signed requests and encrypted assertions supportedBuilt
Which provider a person usesChosen by their email domain, once the domain is proven with a DNS TXT recordBuilt
Multi-factor authenticationThrough your identity providerBuilt (by the provider)
PasswordFor an installation with no identity provider: PBKDF2-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations, at least 12 characters, a lockout after 5 failures in 15 minutes, reset links by mailBuilt
Fresh sign-in for sensitive decisions (step-up)A payment approval needs a sign-in less than five minutes old, by password or through the same identity provider; the decision keeps a fingerprint of itBuilt
InvitesAn admin invites by email; the invite holds a hashed single-use token; a person who already has an account signs in firstBuilt

Once you are signed in, you hold a short-lived token that renews itself for up to 8 hours. Every service checks the token for itself against the public keys that platform-service publishes, rather than trusting another service's word.

  • 0 minutes: You sign in and platform-service issues an access token, signed with Ed25519
  • 15 minutes: The access token expires
    • A rotating refresh token renews it. If a refresh token is used a second time, it is refused and the attempt is recorded in the audit log.
  • 8 hours: The session ends and you sign in again

Roles

Each person holds a role in every team they belong to. A role is a grid that crosses 19 areas (agents, workflows, tools, secrets and egress, files, documents, reviews, cases, settings, access, audit and others) with 8 actions (view, create, edit, publish, delete, run, decide, manage). Every permission check in every service reads that grid. Because no code looks at a role's name, what a role may do is always what its grid says.

RoleWhat it may do in the team
AdminEverything in the team. Actions reserved for the Security team still need a role there
BuilderReads the team's work; creates, edits, tests and publishes its agents, workflows, tools and knowledge
ReviewerReads the team's work and decides its reviews and tasks; in the Security team, decides tool module security reviews
ViewerReads the team's work and chats with its agents
Security adminChanges the outbound allow-list, credentials and storage for every team, and decides tool module security reviews
Chat userChats with the team's agents

Approval tokens are signed with a shared key that the agents and tools services both hold. Signing with an asymmetric key that only the reviews code holdsPlanned

Approval settings

Every way approvals behave is controlled by a setting or a permission. For the full list, with each setting's default, who can change it, where they change it and the code that owns it, see Roles and permissions › Approvals.

The tool gateway

Every call to one of your systems, whether it reads data or changes it, goes through the tools service. Agents and workflows hold no credentials of their own and cannot open their own connections, so each call meets the same checks.

ControlWhat holdsStatus
RegistryOperations come from tool modules: imported from OpenAPI 3.0 or 3.1, discovered from an MCP server, or written by a builder. A module's major change opens a Security review; calls keep the published shape until the new version is publishedBuilt
ConnectionsHow the platform signs in to a system, one account at a time: API key, basic or bearer, OAuth client credentials, OAuth authorization code with PKCE, either OAuth kind proving the app with a signed client assertion instead of a secret, a signed service-account JWT grant (DocuSign, Google), client certificate (mutual TLS). The signing key is sealed like a client secret and never read back; reads show the certificate's thumbprint and expiry. Tokens are stored encrypted and refreshed one at a timeBuilt
Each person signing in to a system with their own accountTools a person runs, and agents acting for them, use that person's own account of the App; a run waiting for an account it does not have becomes a Human Task (Apps)Built

A write on a test account never waits, whatever the team holds; a test run's write on a live account meets the rules a live write meets. A test run with a saved mock answer for its input gets that answer insteadBuilt

When a team asks the person in the chat, each write of an app asks that person first with Allow, Deny and Allow for this chat; only the person who asked answers it. A write on a test account never asks. Writes any approval holds go to a reviewer as before; workflows and agent runs with nobody in them are not asked; a tool the team turned off is refused with Turn on for an admin and Ask an admin for anyone elseBuilt

Audit and evidence

Ops AI records every security-relevant change and every call to an outside system. The records are:

  • the audit log
  • the tool call log
  • the credential, allow-list, connection and storage audits
  • the run journal
  • each review decision
  • the model call log

When someone saves or clears a workflow's schedule, the audit log shows the old and the new schedule written out in words. For the details of each record and its status, see Data and database.

With and without these controls

When a reviewer asks who approved a change and which hosts the agent reached, the answer depends on whether these controls are in place.

  • Without these controls: Each agent is reviewed on its own, from its code.
    • One unreviewed change to a customer's account could be enough to end the pilot
    • Answering an auditor's question can take days of reading code
  • With Ops AI: You answer by pointing to a row in a log.
    • Each action that changes data waits for a named person, who approves the exact input they saw
    • No host is reachable until a Security admin adds it to the list

Platform hardening

ItemWhat holds
NetworkOnly the entry point publishes a port. On Kubernetes, a network policy admits platform-service's private port only from the other services
ContainersNon-root (uid 10001). On Kubernetes: every capability dropped, no privilege escalation, read-only root filesystem except the console, the runtime's default seccomp profile
DatabaseOne login per service with row rights on its own tables only; no running container can change the schema when your DBA applies it
Service callsEach service signs its calls with its own Ed25519 key, and a callee accepts only the calls that caller is allowed to make. An id placed in a call's path (a file the model names to read_file, a tool name) is sent as one encoded path segment, and an id holding a slash or made of dots names no file, so it cannot reach another route
File content given to the modelAn attached file's pages and knowledge passages go in labelled data blocks the model is told never to follow. Text in them that opens or closes a data block, in any letter case or spacing, is escaped, so a file cannot end its block early or forge a knowledge passage
Oversized filesThe reader and the page images share the same limits: at most 2,000 pages, a page drawn at most 16 million pixels (a larger page at a lower resolution), an image frame over 50 million pixels never decoded, and 60 seconds per page in a background read
Plugins in an imageEach pin is a full commit plus the sha256 digest of the plugin's folder; the build refuses a pin with no digest or a download that differs from it (Plugins)
Policy engineThe gateway writes its policy into the policy engine at start and reports unhealthy if the engine serves a different one; token expiry is judged by the gateway's clock
TelemetryNone. Nothing in the platform calls home

11Models

This page shows you how to point every agent at your own model endpoint, and how to cap what each agent may spend and which data it may receive.

Why one provider key per agent is hard to manage

If your team gives each agent its own provider key, you cannot easily tell what one chat cost, which agent used up the budget, or whether a confidential document went to a model that was never cleared for it. Teams also want different models for different work. A lending team may want a private model for borrower files, while a marketing team is happy with a cheaper public one. And when a key leaks, rotating it means finding every agent that held it.

Ops AI avoids this by sending every model call through one internal service, the AI gateway (models-service). That covers an agent's turn, a workflow's AI step and a document read alike. For each call, the gateway knows which key is calling, what that key may still spend, which model a name points at, and how sensitive the data is that the model may receive. Each service holds a model key, and no service holds your provider's credential.

How to set it up

  1. Connect your endpoint. Your operator binds an alias such as default to a model on any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and records its price and the highest data level it may receive.
  2. Save the provider's key once. Your account admin saves it under Settings › Model providers. No team can see it after that.
  3. Issue a capped key per caller. Agents, documents and each workflow get their own model key, each with its own budget and rate limit.
  4. Read the call log. Every call records its tokens, cost, latency and outcome. The log never stores the prompt or the answer text.

Trying it before you have a provider

You can try the platform without a provider or a key, because the release package includes a test model that answers from fixed rules. When you are ready for a real endpoint, your operator binds the alias with the connect-model command (Connect a model). The command prints a model key once, so save it when it appears.

Aliases

An alias is a name such as default that agents, workflows and document types use instead of a provider's model id. Each alias has versions, and the newest current version is the one that serves calls. A version records:

  • the provider connection and the provider's model
  • its price per million input and output tokens
  • the highest data sensitivity it is cleared for
  • whether it may receive images and files

To move an alias to another model, you add a new version. No agent needs to change, because agents refer to the alias rather than the model.

ItemStatus
OpenAI-compatible endpoints: any provider or private gateway that serves the OpenAI chat completions API, streamed or not, with tool callsBuilt
Chat and embedding aliases, versioned, with prices and clearanceBuilt
Embeddings through the same keys, budgets and clearance as chat (POST /v1/models/embeddings)Built

ControlWhat holdsStatus

Data sensitivity

Each alias version is cleared for one level: public, internal, confidential or restricted. A call may name the level of the data it carries, and the gateway refuses the call when the alias is not cleared for that level. The same applies to images and file parts: an alias that is not cleared for them refuses them. Every call records how many images and files it carried.

ItemStatus
The gateway's check of a call's level against the alias's clearanceBuilt
Callers marking each call with the level of its dataPlanned today every call is treated as internal, so an alias must be cleared for internal to serve
Page images for document reads only where the document type, the team's policy and the alias all allow themBuilt

With and without the gateway

Your agents answer through the alias default, and a reviewer's questions about cost and data are answered from one log.

  • Agents hold provider keys: Each agent carries a key to your provider.
    • A single leaked key exposes the whole provider account
    • You cannot cap spend per caller
    • Nothing checks whether confidential data is going to a model that was never cleared for it
  • Through the AI gateway: Agents hold only a capped model key, and the provider's key is held in one place.
    • Moving the alias to another model is one new version, and no agent changes
    • A key at its cap is refused with key_budget_exhausted and the refusal is logged
    • What a chat cost is answered from the call log

The test model

The release package includes a stand-in model endpoint. It speaks the same OpenAI-compatible API and answers from fixed rules, either with plain text or with a tool call when a rule matches the message. Because it calls no provider, it costs nothing. Use it to try the platform before your model endpoint is ready, and for automated checks, but not in production. Each release's automated use cases run on it, so testing makes no real model calls.

It answersWhen
A rule's tool call or textThe person's message matches a rule's when pattern and the rule's tool is offered. Each rule is {when, tool, arguments} or {when, text}, with after and result to chain a step after a tool's result
A call of the tool namedNo rule matches and the message says call <tool> for a tool the agent holds: call <tool> {json} calls it with that JSON object as its input, call <tool> alone with none. Arguments that are not one JSON object are answered as text saying so
The gist of a tool's resultThe last message is a tool's result and no rule follows it
A sentence naming the agent and the messageAnything else

You can try a new tool without writing a rule for it. Open a chat with an agent that holds the tool and type call <tool> {json}.

13Install

Install Ops AI for a team on your own infrastructure. On one machine, the install script does every step and checks the result; on a cluster, or when you run each step yourself, the same images start from Compose or Kubernetes files. Version 1.2.0 is the current release, and its images are published at ghcr.io/chanl-ai/ops-ai.

To try Ops AI on a laptop rather than install it for a team, use the Quickstart: it runs from a clone with a test model and a sample team.

cd ops-ai
./install.sh

To run it unattended, put the answers in a file, one KEY=value per line, and add --yes. Flags win over the file.

./install.sh --answers install-answers.env --yes

When it finishes it prints the address and how to sign in as the first admin.

What it does

  1. Gets the images for linux/amd64 or linux/arm64 from ghcr.io/chanl-ai/ops-ai. --offline <images.tar.gz> loads them from a release package instead, for a machine with no registry access.
  2. Writes the settings file ops-ai.env, readable only by its owner, and generates every key into it. No secret is printed.
  3. Waits for your DBA in dba mode: it writes the database scripts and each login's password to ./dba/, prints the three psql commands to run, and checks the schema before it goes on (Database).
  4. Starts everything and waits for each health check. A model key you give is stored in Ops AI's credential store, never in ops-ai.env.
  5. Checks the install: health through the published port, the sign-in page, a sign-in as the first admin, and one read from every service.

Running ./install.sh again on a working install checks it and changes nothing. It never replaces existing keys, because the secrets key in ops-ai.env unlocks every stored credential.

The other commands

Run them from the folder the install ran in.

CommandWhat it does
./install.sh statusVersion, image source, database and model, each container's state, then the check
./install.sh logs [service]The last 200 lines, followed on a terminal
./install.sh backup [--out DIR]One archive of the database, the stored files and ops-ai.env (Back up and restore)
./install.sh restore <file>Puts a backup back and checks (Back up and restore)
./install.sh upgrade [--version V]Backs up, moves to version V, checks, and rolls back on a failed check (Upgrade)
./install.sh uninstallAsks, then removes the containers; asks again before deleting the data. Keeps ops-ai.env

In dba mode, backup, restore and upgrade need a database admin login that may dump the database, in a file: --admin-url-file <file> holding postgresql://admin:password@host:5432/db. The services' own logins cannot dump it.

Turn on a feature flag

A feature that is not yet released to every install ships behind a flag and is off. To turn one on, list it in ops-ai.env and run ./install.sh again to apply the change.

OPS_FLAGS=mcp_gateway,tool_search
FlagTurns on
mcp_gatewayThe MCP address outside assistants (Claude, Cursor, Copilot) use to reach a team's tools, and the console's MCP channel
tool_searchAgents with many tools search for the one they need
plugin_updatesEach team keeps the plugin version it took and reviews an upgrade before its tools change
area_tabsThe console shows one area at a time, picked from the top bar

A name Ops AI does not know stops every service at start with the list of known flags, so a typo never reads as off.

Set the embedding model

Knowledge search by meaning uses one embedding model per install, set in ops-ai.env.

SettingDefaultWhat it does
OPS_EMBEDDING_ALIASbank-embedThe model alias of kind embedding; bind it to your provider's embedding model the way Connect a model binds a chat model
OPS_EMBEDDING_WIDTH1536The vector width. Above 1,998 every service refuses to start, since no vector index holds it

Changing either one embeds the stored knowledge again; no source is read again. Without an embedding model, search runs on keywords alone and says so in each result. Your own PostgreSQL needs the vector extension (pgvector 0.5 or newer) offered; the built-in database has it.

Install from a company registry

When the machine reaches only your own registry, mirror the images there and point the script at it:

SettingWhat it movesDefault
OPS_IMAGE_REGISTRY, in the shell that runs the scriptWhere the Ops AI images are pulled fromghcr.io/chanl-ai/ops-ai
OPS_BASE_IMAGE_PREFIX, in ops-ai.envA registry prefix ending in / for third-party images, such as PostgreSQL and the policy engineDocker Hub

A machine with no registry at all uses --offline with a release package's image file.

Limits

  • Proven on Docker Desktop for macOS; a run on a Linux server is not yet recorded.
  • An upgrade across two releases that change the schema has not run yet: 1.0.0 is the first release.

Other ways to install

WayUse it when
