The command line on its own

To script Ops AI from a machine that does not run it, install only the opsai command, including behind a company package mirror or with no network: Install the command line.

14Install the command line

Why a terminal helps once a team grows

A console is the right place to look at a run. It is the wrong place to keep forty agent definitions, apply the same change to staging and production, or let a pipeline publish after a review. Without a command line, every change is a sequence of clicks that nobody can compare, repeat or hand to a colleague, and the definitions live only in the database. With one, you can script your team's agents, workflows, knowledge, apps and tasks from a terminal and keep them in version control.

The opsai command line works against an Ops AI install that someone else runs. It installs on its own, without the platform. It needs only Python 3.11 or newer and two small packages, so you can also install it through a company package mirror, or with no network at all. The steps below install it, sign you in and check that it works.

Install

The package is not on the public Python index yet, so you install it from a clone or from the wheel your operator gives you. Publishing it is planned.

From a clone of the repository, with uv or pip:

uv tool install ./sdk/python             # or: python -m pip install --user ./sdk/python
opsai --help                             # prints "usage: opsai ..." and the areas

From a wheel your operator built, or a company index that holds it:

uv tool install ops-ai                   # or: python -m pip install --user ops-ai

The package is ops-ai and the command is opsai. The package also installs an ops command for one release, which only prints a message that opsai is the new name.

If your shell cannot find opsai after the install, its folder is not on your PATH. Run uv tool update-shell and open a new shell, or add ~/.local/bin (where pip installs on Linux and macOS) to your PATH.

Sign in

opsai login --base-url https://ops.example.com --email you@example.com
opsai people me

opsai login asks for your password and saves the address, your team and the session in a profile, which every later command and the Python client read. The session renews itself, and no token is ever printed.

SettingWhat it doesDefault
--profile NAME or OPS_PROFILEKeeps several sign-ins side by side, such as staging and productiondefault
OPS_BASE_URLThe Ops AI address, when no profile holds onenone
OPS_CONFIGReads profiles from another filethe profile file in your home folder
--team IDActs in another of your teamsthe team saved at sign-in
--jsonPrints JSON instead of a table, on every commandoff

Through a company mirror

Point uv or pip at your mirror's Python index. For Sonatype Nexus the index is https://<nexus-host>/repository/<repo-name>/simple/, so include the trailing /simple/.

SettingForNotes
UV_DEFAULT_INDEX (or UV_INDEX_URL)uvReplaces the public index
PIP_INDEX_URLpipPIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL adds a second index
SSL_CERT_FILE (also PIP_CERT)A company CA certificate, as a PEM fileUV_NATIVE_TLS=1 makes uv use the operating system's certificates instead
PIP_TRUSTED_HOST / UV_INSECURE_HOSTA host without valid TLSPrefer a CA certificate
export UV_DEFAULT_INDEX=https://nexus.example.com/repository/pypi-group/simple/
export SSL_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/company-ca.pem
uv tool install ./sdk/python

Keep credentials out of URLs in shared files, because a URL with a password shows up in logs and shell history. Use a ~/.netrc file (machine nexus.example.com login <user> password <token>, mode 600), which uv and pip both read, or uv's UV_INDEX_<NAME>_USERNAME and UV_INDEX_<NAME>_PASSWORD with a named index.

If a firewall policy on the mirror blocks packages, allow the ones below, which the command line needs, at any version in range:

PackageVersions acceptedNewest tested
httpx0.27 up to, not including, 1.00.28.1
typing-extensions4.12 or newer4.16.0
httpcoreany that httpx accepts (1.x)1.0.9
h11any that httpcore accepts0.16.0
anyioany that httpx accepts (4.x)4.16.0
idnaany that anyio and httpx accept3.20
certifiany2026.10.23

Installing from a clone also builds the package, which needs hatchling, packaging, pathspec, pluggy and trove-classifiers from the mirror. Installing a built wheel needs none of them.

With no network

On a machine with internet, put the wheel and its dependencies in one folder:

python -m pip wheel --no-deps --wheel-dir wheelhouse ./sdk/python
python -m pip download --dest wheelhouse httpx typing-extensions

Copy the folder to the target machine and install from it alone:

uv tool install --no-index --find-links wheelhouse ops-ai     # or: python -m pip install --user --no-index --find-links wheelhouse ops-ai
opsai --help

To build the folder for other operating systems or Python versions than the one you are on, or to upload it to a Nexus hosted repository, see Install from a company registry.

What success looks like

opsai --help prints the areas, and opsai people me prints you and your team. From then on a definition is a file: validate it, apply it, and review the change in your repository like any other.

15Operate

Keep an install healthy once it runs: check it and read its logs, move it to a new release, back it up, and rotate its keys. The install script's commands come first on each page; the Compose and Kubernetes commands follow for installs made by hand.

Check the install

./install.sh status

It prints the version, image source, database and model, each container's state, then runs the install check: health through the published port, the sign-in page, a sign-in as the first admin, and one read from every service.

CheckComposeKubernetesHealthy
Every container$C pskubectl -n ops-ai get podsEach service healthy or ready; the schema job exited 0
The entry pointcurl -fsS https://<your host>/api/platform/v1/healthSame{"status":"ok"}
Sign-inOpen your address and sign inSameThe console opens

Here $C is your Compose command, for example docker compose -p ops-ai -f deploy/compose/app.yaml --env-file ops-ai.env.

ContainerUnhealthy means
agentsThe database is unreachable, or no model is connected: it answers 503 until one is
toolsThe policy engine does not serve the gateway's own policy: it answers 503 policy_drift

any other serviceThe process is down

Read the logs

TaskScriptComposeKubernetes
One service./install.sh logs agents$C logs -f agentskubectl -n ops-ai logs deploy/agents -f
Every service./install.sh logs$C logs --since 1hkubectl -n ops-ai logs deploy/<service> --since 1h
The schema job./install.sh logs migrate$C logs migratekubectl -n ops-ai logs job/migrate

Each line is one JSON object with the time, level, event, service, and the request, tenant and team ids. Secret values are masked before the line is written.

What to watch

SignalWhy it mattersHealthy
The work queueRuns waiting to be claimed mean the workers are busy or downClaimed within a second or two
Crashed and recovered runsEach crash runs a step and its model calls againRare, each followed by a recovery
Tool calls left runningThe gateway stopped mid-write, so the effect on your system is unknownNone; each needs a person to check the system it called
Overdue human tasksPeople are not keeping up with the queueWithin the deadlines your workflows set
Model spend against budgetsA spent key stops new workBelow each key's cap
Database size and write loadSaved run state grows with open workSteady; vacuum on a schedule
ClockLeases and timers use the database's clockHosts within a few seconds of it

Scale

PartHow it scales
Workflow runsAdd worker processes. Each runs 4 runs at once from the shared queue; a run waiting for a person holds no worker
The APIsEvery service except files and knowledge is stateless, so more replicas can run behind the proxy or a Service
Files and knowledgeOne replica each, since their bytes are on a volume one replica writes
Crash recoveryA run's lease expires 15 seconds after its worker stops, and another worker continues from its last saved step

Upgrade with the script

git fetch --tags && git checkout v<new version>
./install.sh upgrade

The script backs up, gets the new images, applies the schema, restarts, and checks. If the check fails, it restores the backup on the old version and exits with an error. At the version already running, it checks and changes nothing. --version V picks a version other than the checkout's.

In dba mode it writes the upgrade scripts to ./dba/upgrade-<from>-to-<to>/, waits for your DBA to apply them, and needs --admin-url-file <file> to take the backup.

Upgrade by hand

  1. Back up the database and the stored files (Back up and restore).
  2. Upgrade the database. Your DBA applies the new release's upgrade-roles.sql, then upgrade.sql as the schema owner, then the new release's grants.sql (Database).
  3. Start the new images.
InstallCommand
ComposeSet OPS_IMAGE_TAG to the new version, then docker compose -p ops-ai -f deploy/compose/app.yaml --env-file ops-ai.env up -d (add -f deploy/compose/dba.yaml in DBA mode). Without a DBA, the schema job applies the upgrade before the services start
KubernetesSet the new tag in the overlay, then kubectl -n ops-ai delete job migrate and kubectl apply -k <overlay>, since a finished Job cannot change

How it behaves

  • Every service checks the database's schema version at start and refuses one it does not match, naming the upgrade that is missing. Two releases cannot be mixed by mistake.
  • Each step of upgrade.sql checks the version it starts from and stops before any change when the database is somewhere else, so running it twice is refused.
  • Some steps move rows that the running release still writes. Stop the services before the database step, and start only the new release after it. Agents 0120 (stored skill step tools) does not need the stop: it rewrites skill and agent versions one batch per transaction, each batch setting its table's policy aside and putting it back, so the services keep serving. A version the earlier release saves after its last pass is refused by the publish check and the attach until its builder marks the step's tool.

Roll back

Migrations do not roll back on their own. Either restore the backup taken before the upgrade, or have your DBA run the release's downgrade.sql where every step has one; then start the previous images. The script does this for you when its check fails.

Back up and restore with the script

./install.sh backup
./install.sh restore backups/<file>.tar.gz

A backup is one archive in ./backups/, readable only by its owner, holding a dump of the database, the files and knowledge volumes, and ops-ai.env. --out DIR writes it elsewhere. A restore stops the services, recreates the database from the dump, puts the volumes back, starts everything and runs the install check. It refuses a backup made with another secrets key.

In dba mode both commands need --admin-url-file <file>: the services' own logins cannot dump the database under its tenant policies.

A backup holds ops-ai.env and its keys. Keep it as safe as the database: OPS_SECRETS_KEY unlocks every stored credential, and without it a restored install cannot call your systems.

Back up and restore by hand

Back up the database as the server admin, with your usual PostgreSQL tools or, on Azure, automated backups and point-in-time restore. A dump as the schema owner stops with a row-level security error, because the tenant policies apply to the owner too.

docker run --rm -e PGPASSWORD=<admin password> -v "$PWD/backup:/backup" postgres:17 \
  pg_dump -Fc -f /backup/ops.dump "host=<host> port=5432 user=<admin> dbname=ops sslmode=require"
docker run --rm -v ops-ai_files-data:/data -v "$PWD/backup:/out" alpine tar czf /out/files-data.tgz -C /data .
docker run --rm -v ops-ai_kb-data:/data -v "$PWD/backup:/out" alpine tar czf /out/kb-data.tgz -C /data .

Keep a copy of the settings file, or at least OPS_SECRETS_KEY, with each backup.

To restore into a new database, stop the services, then:

psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 "host=<host> port=5432 user=<admin> dbname=postgres sslmode=require" \
  -c "CREATE DATABASE ops_restored OWNER ops_migrator"
docker run --rm -e PGPASSWORD=<admin password> -v "$PWD/backup:/backup" postgres:17 \
  pg_restore --exit-on-error -d "host=<host> port=5432 user=<admin> dbname=ops_restored sslmode=require" /backup/ops.dump
docker run --rm -v ops-ai_files-data:/data -v "$PWD/backup:/in" alpine sh -c "rm -rf /data/* && tar xzf /in/files-data.tgz -C /data"
docker run --rm -v ops-ai_kb-data:/data -v "$PWD/backup:/in" alpine sh -c "rm -rf /data/* && tar xzf /in/kb-data.tgz -C /data"

Point each service's database setting at ops_restored, keep the same keys in the settings file, and start everything again.

What to back up where

InstallDatabaseFiles and knowledge bytes
Script or Composepg_dump as the server adminThe files-data and kb-data volumes
Kubernetespg_dump as the server adminVolume snapshots of the files and kb claims
Files in S3 or Azure BlobAs aboveThe store's own versioning or replication

Rotate keys

KeySteps
Approval key (OPS_REVIEW_KEY)Set the new value for agents and tools and restart both. Approvals in flight must be given again
A service's signing keyGive the service a new key and key id, add its public key to every other service's trusted list beside the old one, restart the others, then the service; then remove the old key id and restart the others again
Sign-in token key (OPS_PLATFORM_SIGNING_KEY)Set a new key and key id and restart every service; people may need to sign in again
Secrets key (OPS_SECRETS_KEY)Changing it makes every stored credential unreadable, so each must be entered again. A rotation that re-encrypts them is planned
A provider's model keyA Security admin replaces it in the credential store; no restart
Database passwordsChange each login's password, update its setting, restart that service

Remove

./install.sh uninstall asks, then removes the containers, and asks again before deleting the data. It keeps ops-ai.env. By hand: docker compose ... down keeps the volumes and down -v deletes them; on Kubernetes, kubectl delete -k <overlay> removes the volume claims with it.

Limits

  • An upgrade across two releases that change the schema has not run yet: 1.0.0 is the first release.
  • Metrics are planned; health checks and logs are built.
  • Ops AI schedules no backups; run the backup from your scheduler or use your database's own.

16Azure SQL

A full install of Ops AI on Azure SQL Database or SQL Server is not yet proven. Install on PostgreSQL today; Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server is supported. The SQL Server scripts are ready for your DBA to review now, so the review can run in parallel with the remaining work.

Azure SQL Database and SQL Server 2025 are the second database Ops AI is built for. Each service reaches the database only through its own store, and the places where the two databases differ (locking, queue claims, inserts that update an existing row, the clock, the tenant of a transaction) sit in one layer, so the services above the stores do not change. On every change, continuous integration runs the store, service kit and identity suites, and each service's store and isolation tests, on SQL Server 2025 beside PostgreSQL, and fails when a SQL Server case is skipped.

Ready for review

ItemWhat it holdsStatus
roles.sqlRun in master as a server administrator: one SQL login per service plus the schema owner ops_migrator, each password a sqlcmd variable; the database with collation Latin1_General_100_BIN2_UTF8 and READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON, owned by ops_migratorBuilt
One script per service, and bundle.sqlEvery table, index, key and default, the version table stamped at the release, and a security policy per tenant table. The bundle refuses a database with another collation, without read-committed snapshot, or below compatibility level 160Built
grants.sqlA database user per service login with SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on its own tables and nothing else; the one system user the background loops switch to, which only the agents login may impersonate, with the same narrow grants as on PostgreSQLBuilt
manifest.json and SHA256SUMSThe commit, each service's schema version, every file's checksumBuilt
Tenant isolationA security policy on each tenant table of the agents and platform services: a filter predicate on reads and block predicates after insert and after update, reading the tenant from SESSION_CONTEXT, which the services set and clear per transactionBuilt in the scripts
Data typesText as VARCHAR(max) under the UTF-8 collation, JSON as NVARCHAR(max), timestamps as DATETIMEOFFSET, booleans as BIT, keys named as on PostgreSQL so later upgrades name the same objectsBuilt
Upgrade scriptsGenerated per release pair the same way as for PostgreSQL, each step guarded by the version it starts fromBuilt
How the scripts are kept rightCompiled from each service's table definitions, which tests hold equal to what the PostgreSQL migrations build, and compared on every change with reviewed copiesBuilt

Your DBA runs them with sqlcmd -b, which stops at the first error:

sqlcmd -b -d master -i roles.sql -v database=ops ops_migrator_password=<...> ops_agents_runtime_password=<...>
sqlcmd -b -U ops_migrator -d ops -i bundle.sql
sqlcmd -b -U ops_migrator -d ops -i grants.sql

17What's built today

Check what runs before you plan around it

You are deciding whether Ops AI covers your use case, and a feature list that mixes working and hoped-for items does not help you. If you plan around a capability that is only designed, you can lose months. Every row below says which kind it is, and each row is read from the code of this release. Built means the feature runs and an automated use case or test covers it. Partial means part of it runs, and the row says which part. Planned means it is designed and not yet in the code. Read the area your use case touches, then start with the Quickstart to try what is built.

19Watch a folder

Files that live in an app, such as a SharePoint library of policies or supplier invoices, change all the time, and copying them by hand means the copy goes stale. Watch a folder to have Files bring them in for you: one entry per file, and a new version each time the file changes in the app.

Try it

You need the app turned on for your team and signed in (Set up an app), and the Builder or Admin role.

  1. Open Data › Files and choose the Watched folders tab.
  2. Select Watch a folder.
  3. Name it, for example "Supplier invoices", and pick the app. Select Next.
  4. Pick the sites, libraries or folders to include. Each list searches by name. Add a rule under Include or Exclude to narrow it further; a rule starts with /, and Exclude wins. Select Next.
  5. Read the review. It names the folders you picked. Files lists what it found after you select Check now. Select Watch a folder.
  6. Nothing is copied yet. On the folder's row, open the menu and select Check now. The row shows Checking…, and a moment later it shows when the check ran and how many files it brought in.

The files are now in All files, marked as coming from a watched folder. Open one to see which folder it came from and its place in the app.

How it works

  • One entry per file. A file keeps one entry in Files however often it changes. When a check finds a changed file it adds a new version to that entry and keeps the earlier one. A check takes the newest version of each file, so a file changed three times between two checks arrives as one new version.
  • A renamed or moved file stays the same entry.
  • A file removed from the folder is marked as removed at the source. Files keeps it and its versions.
  • Each check reads from the app on your team's connection. If the app refuses the sign-in or cannot be reached, the check stops, nothing is lost, and the page says why and what to do. Reconnecting the app is on its page under Data › Apps.
  • Everyone on the team can read the files that arrive, whatever access they have in the app. Files records who may see each file in the app but does not apply it yet. Pick folders the whole team may see.

Failed files

A check that cannot bring one file in names it in the In Files column of the folder's row, with its size and the reason. The other files in the check still arrive.

ReasonWhat it meansWhat to do
Larger than 25 MBA watched folder takes files up to 25 MBSplit the file or make it smaller in the app, or upload it to Files directly with Upload on All files. A file that is made smaller is tried again on the next check
Could not be fetchedThe app did not hand over that one fileThe next checks try it again, up to three times. If it still fails, change the file in the app or upload it directly

A file larger than the limit is listed once with its size. It is listed again only if the file changes.

A check that stopped part way says Partial and why, for example that the app slowed the check down or that the folder is long. The next check carries on from there.

Check now, change and stop

ActionWhat it does
Check nowRuns a check at once. A folder that is already being checked says so instead of starting a second one
Change foldersChanges the name or the folders picked. The new folders are read whole on the next check. The app stays the same: to use another connection, add a new watched folder
Stop watchingFiles stops checking this folder. The files already brought in stay in Files, with their versions, and keep following their retention rules like any other file. Files that change in the app after that are not brought in

Stopping is in the folder's row menu. Files never deletes a brought-in file because you stopped watching; delete a file from All files if you want it gone.

Who may do what

WhoCan
Admin and BuilderWatch a folder, change its folders, check it now and stop watching it. Each is recorded in the audit log with the folders named
Anyone who can see FilesRead the list of watched folders, their last check and the files that arrived. They see no buttons for the actions above

Limits

  • A check runs when someone presses Check now. Checks on a schedule are planned.
  • SharePoint and OneDrive are the apps a folder can be watched from today. Others are planned.
  • A file over 25 MB is not brought in.
  • A workflow that starts when a watched folder brings in a file is planned.
